utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Terzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the beginning of your evidence will continue to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I just have two or three more questions I wanted to ask you in connection with the VJ Commission For Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. In some of the stories that were reported about the commission, one of the allegations that was made was that the members of the commission were being paid something on the order of 350 dinars per hour for their work on the commission. Any truth to that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly now, but it's probably around that figure per hour. But on a monthly basis they received a maximum of 2 to 300 euros, so you can do your math. I don't want the wrong picture to be created here. The commission was not a unit of the General Staff or of the Ministry of Defence. There weren't any permanently employed people there. Everybody worked there in addition to their regular duties. It was only the secretary of the commission who was there every day and also a typist who was a secretary at the time as well, and the rest met several times a month whenever necessary; that is to say, when requests would come in, to have them studied and to see who they should be forwarded to. When the materials would arrive and the responses from the General Staff and from the Ministry of Defence, then this was also supposed to be studied and the proposals were supposed to be made for the Ministry of Defence and the Chief of General Staff, and at first it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I think you've answered my question. Do you recall at that time between 2001 and 2003, what was the average monthly salary in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This was a lot of money at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the average hourly pay for professors at the military academy. This had to do mostly with generals, so that is why they were paid according to that criterion. I'm talking about professors who were not permanently employed at the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I think you told us yesterday that most of the generals who were on this commission with you were still active-duty. So was this 350 dinars per hour paid to them in addition to their regular military salary?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only those who were not in professional service received this fee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many of those were there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said yesterday, it was only General Gojovic, and I'm not sure whether General Farkas was retired at the point when the commission started working or whether he was retired later, I'm not sure about that. Later on because of the growing needs that I started talking about a few moments ago, that is to say giving elementary assistance to people who turned to the commission, General Obrencevic was also engaged and later General Milos Gojkovic as well. Before that, one of them was the chief military prosecutor and the other one the president of the military court. They only worked in connection with the persons that you were asking for, seven accused, about 20 suspects, most of them were required as witnesses and some did not really have a status. They turned to the commission for this elementary legal assistance because they had no one else to turn to. These three persons gave the elementary assistance that was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who are you talking about in that answer when you say "these persons didn't have anyone else to turn to," you're talking about accused appearing before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the accused. We did not have any contact with the accused at that time. It was only suspects and witnesses, mostly witnesses turned to us because quite simply they were in a situation especially before the law on cooperation with the Tribunal was passed, I mean at the time when the state had not regulated its relationship with the Tribunal they were in a very unpleasant situation. If they went to testify they would clash with the law that made it incumbent on them to guard secrets and if they didn't go they faced other risks. So then they turned to this commission because they didn't really have anybody else to turn to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in your earlier answer, page 3, line 11, when you were talking about Gojkovic and others you said they only worked in connection with the persons you were asking for, seven accused, about 20 suspects, most of them were required as witnesses. So did they or did they not provide some assistance to accused?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat once again that the accused did not turn to the commission, as far as I know, none of the accused then -- well, maybe I'm mistaken, but none of the accused then -- well, I'm not sure now. I don't know whether any of them were still at large, whether they were moving about freely. I repeat once again it was primarily witnesses that turned to us and some suspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: About --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, you did say seven accused, according to our transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No -- well, I mentioned that just in the context of the Office of the Prosecutor looking for some 100 people then, so I just classified them, seven accused, about 20 suspects; as for the rest, most of them witnesses. But their status was not quite regulated so I did not include the accused in this other category in terms of providing legal assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, now you're talking about people that the Office of the Prosecutor was looking for. Are you talking about providing assistance to fugitives?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. As far as I know, there were only some accused who were fugitives and still are; we did not render any assistance to them, we didn't even have any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Didn't you or the commission provide assistance to Mr. Milosevic in the preparation and presentation of his defence case before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said yesterday, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're aware during his trial that many of his defence witnesses brought in hundreds of documents and exhibits, many of which were documents that were the subject of previous and long-standing OTP requests for those very kinds of documents. You know about that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say in part I did not follow the course of that trial and I cannot say that I know in detail what it was that was going on. But yesterday I said how the commission provided documents to anybody, the OTP or the Defence, through the Ministry of Defence at first and then when the national cooperation for cooperation with the Tribunal was established, then through that national commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday you said at page 15903, line 12 through 17: "Whenever we received a request from the OTP or from one of the Defence teams for that matter, because the commission did not have any documents we would write to all the tactical leaders in the Army of Yugoslavia for them to inform us whether such documents existed to begin with; and secondly, to inform us about their position as to whether these documents could be forwarded or not." In that answer when you say "the tactical leaders," who are you referring to? Are you referring to the military commanders that were in charge of troops during this various conflicts?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents were either in the archives of the Army of Yugoslavia, that is to say those who were no longer used had already been archived in the archives of Yugoslavia, or they were in organisational units of the Ministry of Defence and the General Staff. These were documents that were still being used, and we asked them for these documents. Of course we asked for these documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- From persons who were then in top positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In top positions at the time of the request?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of the request, people who were in top positions. We were not sending this to particular persons but to organisational units; that is to say, that documents are not sent to a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, your answer said you would write to all the tactical leaders. I assume that the tactical leaders are persons?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. But correspondence takes place between two institutions. I say send a letter to the personnel department. I do not write to the head of the personnel department. Of course it is first the chief of the personnel department that has to look at this document, and then he assigns the person who's going to work on that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, for example, if in 2002 or 2003 the OTP was requesting documents about the 3rd Army or, for example, the war diary of the Pristina Corps, when you got that request, who would you write to, meaning you as the commission?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That request would be sent at least to two addresses, one is the military archives if that document had been archived, that is what the archive has to establish; and then the second address would be the command of the 3rd Army. There would be no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And your decision about whether or not the document would be forwarded just depended on what the commander of the 3rd Army told you, correct? If the commander of the 3rd Army said, No, I don't want you to send that to The Hague, you would not send it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about that yesterday. You are referring to the commander of the 3rd Army here. The commander would say in the response whether the document exists or not, and he would provide his opinion if the document does exist whether he believes that it can be submitted to the Office of the Prosecutor or not. Yesterday I said that in many cases when the chief or the commander would say no, that is to say when their opinion was that it should not be provided, this would be discussed by the collegium of the Chief of General Staff, and then we would suggest that these documents be provided on the basis of our knowledge that this document is not of essential interest of the national security of the country. And also we received other materials, rather we would send materials provided that they be given proper protection here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give any examples where the commission overruled the position of a commander who said documents should not be provided?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you answer that. If you look at the previous answer, Mr. Hannis, the discussion is not at the commission, according to this, it's the chief of the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff. So we seem to have got another body involved now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're correct. And there's another correct I need to follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me withdraw that question right now, General, and ask you this question. You said that first you would ask the commander whether or not the document existed, but didn't you tell us he also checked with the archives. So if the document exists in the archive, then the only thing you're asking the commander is what his position is about whether the document should be provided; and when I say "you," I mean either the commission or the collegium. Which one is it that's deciding on the commander's opinion about release of such documents?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you did not exactly repeat what I said. In this specific case that you asked about we would send an inquiry to the military archives and to the command of the army. That is to the military archive because we didn't know if it was archived or not; if it is archived, then the military archives would give us an answer with regard to that document and give us their opinion or position. If the document had not been archived then the command of the 3rd Army would reply whether this document exists or not and provide their position. Since I was subordinated to the Chief of the General Staff, in principle military organisations -- well, I could not and I did not have the right to send any document to some other organ without the knowledge of the Chief of General Staff. I think that is an answer to that question; that is to say that the entire work of the commission was examined at the collegium of the Chief of General Staff and also at briefings with the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So in our hypothetical situation when you got a request from the OTP for documents from the 3rd Army, as I understand it you - and I mean -- I take it in this context it's the commission - makes an inquiry of, number one, the archive about whether or not the document exists; and if it exists, you just said the archive would give you their position about whether it should be released, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you would also make an inquiry from the tactical leader of the 3rd Army at the time of the request about whether or not the document existed with them apparently and their position about whether it should be released, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So in our hypothetical example, if the document is archived and there's also a copy still with the 3rd Army commander, you'll have two opinions then, one from the archive, one from the 3rd Army commander, correct, about whether the document should be released?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. At the moment when a document is archived, all copies are destroyed. So the 3rd Army could not -- I mean I'm talking about normal -- well, I'm not going to rule things out for anybody, including the 3rd Army, that they couldn't have done something against the rules, but according to rules all of it should have been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please be asked to speak into the microphone and slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you also said to my colleague, or rather, it was the collegium that had a discussion and the collegium not a single time changed, amended the proposal of the commission. Every time they accepted the proposal of the Commission, just like the minister of defence did, just like the National Council did except in this one particular case ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. -- I think the answer is sufficient. Mr. Terzic, could you try, please, to speak a little more slowly to assist the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, who was the Chief of Staff of the General Staff of the VJ at this time, between 2001 and 2003?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when the commission existed, the Chief of General Staff in the first period was Colonel-General Nebojsa Pavkovic, and later on Lieutenant-Colonel-General Branko Krga.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at that time if there were requests of the OTP of documents relating to the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army with relation to events in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, General Pavkovic certainly would have a personal interest having been the commander of those respective units at different times in 1998 and 1999, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last topic I want to ask you related to the commission. In your work with the commission do you recall receiving any requests from the OTP or from anyone for documents relating to a body called the Joint Command or the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that there were such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall that the initial responses to those OTP requests indicated that there was no such body for -- if there was such a body it ceased to exist at the end of 1998, late 1998, maybe October, and it never existed in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. As far as this Joint Command is concerned I first learned about it from an OTP request. According to the same principle that I explained, I wrote letters and in keeping with the answers received I sent an answer to you. I did not change anything. The complete archives of the, or rather, the complete documentation of the commission was archived, and in this documentation you can see every answer provided by the commission on the basis of the replies received from the tactical leaders in the archives; namely, every time an answer was provided on the basis of the answers we were given. That was quite understandable to me. "Joint Command" sounded illogical to me, and until that moment, or rather, at that moment I did not try to check whether that was correct or not or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall whether any of those requests for the Joint Command documents were discussed in the collegium?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them went there. I cannot remember whether at the collegium -- let me just explain something.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the speaker because other microphones are on in the courtroom. We're sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, there's a problem hearing you, probably because I've got my microphone on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please start that answer again and just try to speak a little more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is to say all members of the collegium received material for the collegium, and it is certain that that question was in the materials. But now I cannot confirm to you with any certainty whether there was a special debate at the collegium with regard to that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware that the OTP was only able to obtain documents concerning the Joint Command and Joint Command orders for the year 1999 after General Delic came to testify in the Slobodan Milosevic and he brought with him, among his many documents, a document from the Supreme Command Staff entitled: "Suggestions" from General Ojdanic. And in that document it made reference to the Joint Command order of 15 April 1999. It was only after that that we were able to get from Serbia documents regarding the Joint Command in 1999. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this question is not quite correct. General Delic did not bring Suggestions, as Mr. Hannis just said. Let us clarify that. He probably meant some other document but not the document of the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I may have misstated, but it was my understanding that we first became aware of this when there was a reference to a Joint Command order. It may not have been in Suggestions, it may have been in one of his combat reports with a reference to the Joint Command. I apologise if I've misstated that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terzic, you said that you remember these requests and you remember the first response that was sent when Joint Command documents were requested. What was the very first response sent to the OTP in relation to requests for Joint Command documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yesterday when I started dealing with this issue, I pointed out that I'm only talking on the basis of my memory after four and a half years. During the preparations I did not look at a single piece of paper, there was nothing to jog my memory, so it's very hard for me now to go into details and to speak about this period of time because, quite simply, I do not remember. If I'm not mistaken- but I'm not sure - the answer, the first one was that these documents did not exist, that they were not there, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, General, let's move on to another topic. I'd like to show you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that, you're now well in excess of our traditional approach to cross-examination. Is it something that you need to deal with that you're about to move on to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to deal with some of the documents that he talked about in his direct exam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're going to be talking about an extensive -- well, perhaps not. I've got to -- we've got to allow for the fact that there's a statement in this case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I probably wrongly said that you are by now over the limit. You're probably approaching the normal equivalent time. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe I am. Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to move quickly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, in document P1479, this is a Supreme Command Staff order on volunteers dated the 7th of May, 1999, and I think you've seen this before.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you about item number 10 which is on page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. This paragraph says in English: "I prohibit admission of members of paramilitary units, groups, and individuals already present in the zones of responsibility to VJ commands, units, and installations as volunteers without prior completion of procedures regulated by this order." Now, as I read that, that sounds as though there were already some volunteer -- or some paramilitary units or groups present in zones of responsibility to the VJ. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to answer that question because an order, once it's issued, was not sent to me. I was dealing with education pursuant to a decision of the military top. So I can't really confirm or deny this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I read that, that does not appear to be a blanket prohibition to the admission of such paramilitary units as volunteers, but rather that they might be admitted if the other procedures described in the order were followed, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can interpret that in that way, although there were other interpretations possible, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I'd like to show the witness Exhibit P1943, which is a Supreme Command Staff document regarding problems related to dispatching volunteers to the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is signed by Colonel-General Matovic. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you didn't specify the time, the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It should be up on your screen now. It's from the 20th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's talking about some of the problems regarding the processing of volunteers in the Bubanj Potok facility. This relates to the report of problems identified by the 3rd Army in its 10th of April report. Do you know why it took ten days to deal with this rather critical issue?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I'm not mistaken, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff reacted on the 17th [as interpreted] of April when he ordered that certain measures be taken. Among other things, I was ordered to take up the training in the volunteer training centre, and on the 14th of April the chief of Supreme Command Staff signed an order in which all the problems related to the volunteers were put in. I got familiar with this document because I didn't remember it in the proofing for my testimony here, and I can consider that this document is an -- is an attempt on the part of the tactical leader to operationalise this, although the military districts were supposed to get all those documents from the army commander pursuant to the order of the Chief of General Staff of the 14th. It is difficult for me to comment because this is not a military document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, you're being asked yet again by the interpreters to slow down. You must bear that in mind. We cannot continue this way unless you cooperate with us. You referred there to something happening on the 14th of April. Did you mean to say the 14th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 14th of April the Chief of General Staff signed an order, or rather, the chief of Supreme Command Staff, he signed on order that exists in the documents that unified the overall topic of the volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have your order, I was just -- your answer, I was just checking that the date was correct. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I see Mr. Visnjic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 16, line 7, the witness said 11th of April and the transcript reads the 17th of April, so the witness said the Chief of General Staff responded on the 11th of April already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, now I'd like to show you Exhibit P925. These are the minutes of the collegium meeting of the VJ on 27 November 1998, and according to the minutes you were in attendance. Do you recall attending that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time I was not a member of the collegium of the Chief of General Staff, and it is really difficult for me now to remember whether I attended or not. I did attend some of the meetings when they were dealing with the topic from my purview when that was education and training.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to go to page 30 of the English, and I believe it's page 28 of the B/C/S. General, it does appear, according to the minutes, that you were there and that you made -- you made a comment in connection with something that, first of all, General Smiljanic had been talking about. You see -- do you see that reference to General Smiljanic on that page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in. It is impossible for me to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not up to my glasses, it's really illegible. The next paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Actually, I've got a hard copy of that page I could pass to the usher to hand to the witness, if that will assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I'm going to hand you a hard copy. And near the middle of that paragraph General Smiljanic is talking about staff war exercises in the last two years. And he says: "Because we were not clear as to" --

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. He says: "Because we were not clear as to the method of work of the staff in preparing a decision of the Supreme Command ..." And then you speak and you say: "General, the SRV," I don't know what that stands for. Can you tell us what that acronym stands for. It's translated into English as S or S with the diacritic full banana over it as we say. SRV, what is that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Staff war exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But here those who taped it and who typed it up later, they didn't catch everything. I can clarify what it is that I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read this and I'll ask you about that. "General, the SRV at the level of the General Staff and an exercise then showed that the organisation of the General Staff is not adequate at all, the staff and the Supreme Command. Without us knowing what we were doing for three days." Can you tell us what the Supreme Command means in that context?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well in order to answer that question I talked about the staff war exercise that was carried out ten years ago, sometime in 1987 in I'm not mistaken, and I participated there. And from my point of view it is correct during my participation in that exercise a great many people didn't know what they were supposed to do, and that is why I made this comment. And now you're asking me at that time what the word "Supreme Command" meant. I was talking about the staff war exercise at the time when the Supreme Command in 1987 was precisely defined, more precisely defined --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1999 --

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- In the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in 1999 --

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999, it doesn't really make much difference, the constitutional provision was sufficient for me. Let me respond to your question, but I need to clarify. The president of the FRY commanded the army in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. As far as I know, there were no more detailed regulations defining the Supreme Command and what it comprised, but in my mind I saw it as the Supreme Command Staff. I think that I now answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, maybe. You attended collegium meetings in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them, only when training and education were discussed, except after the beginning of the air-strikes and several days after that I started being acting the chief of the administration for training and manning and that's how I participated in the sessions of the collegium of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not meetings but briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go to the last document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you leave that, I have to say I'm not following this. Why was this being discussed at this time, Mr. Terzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's difficult for me to remember now in the context, but it is obvious that Lieutenant-General Spasoje Smiljanic, at that time, if I'm not mistaken, he was the chief of the operations administration and he, of course, by his office asked questions about the ability of the General Staff to deal with the war situation, the wartime capabilities, not the peacetime capabilities. And he proposed that some kind of a staff war exercise be set up at the level of the General Staff. And I as a person who was in charge of training at all levels and in all structures in the Yugoslav Army, I supported that proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you suggesting the start of your comment is about 1987?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In 1987 a staff war exercise was carried out at the level of the General Staff. At that time I worked in the General Staff, I participated in that war exercise, and the experiences I'm talking about come from that exercise. That's why I'm talking about them here. I talk about those experiences in my intervention here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, propose that we listen to the audiotape of the answer the General gave at page 19, line 24, 25, and page 20, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And why do you suggest that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I think that the witness's answer differed from what is recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you say the answer was?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim that the witness said, In my mind I saw it as the Supreme Defence Council, and it says here the "Supreme Command Staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that will be enough for current purposes, Mr. Visnjic, thank you. But what I'm trying to understand, Mr. Terzic, is your suggestion that your reference is to 1987. Are you suggesting that things were disorganized in 1987?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The General Staff, at least in the Yugoslav Army at that time rarely carried out staff war exercises, unlike all other levels of command. I think that this is a similar occurrence in all armies of the world, and at all other command levels there are quite specific rules and instructions for their work if there is a war. For the highest level of command, such instructions do not exist because they would hamper the initiatives and the decision-making so that because those things were carried out very rarely, in 1987 those people who were employed at the General Staff in this three-day staff war exercise, they did not really do all that well. In the meantime so between 1987 and this year that is mentioned here, there were no staff war exercises, and I'm trying to say that there had been a long time and probably again the officers who were working at the General Staff again at the beginning would not do that well, they would be a bit confused, and it would be necessary to organize a staff war exercise for people to get some kind of a refresher course and to be able to carry their wartime duties in a much better fashion. I'm not talking about their peacetime duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I'm not understanding is that in the second paragraph you go on to suggest the Supreme Command was organized the way it was in 1987, which doesn't seem to be consistent with the idea that you had a problem with in 1987.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1987, according to the constitution of the then-Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia, this issue was quite specifically regulated. Here I'm talking about the same thing that I said in my evidence here. In 1987 there were no specific regulations as to what the Supreme Command was, and that is why I am making this suggestion that this be regulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying clearly that this discussion is not about recent problems but problems of 12 years before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I suggest that that -- there's some problem with that. General Smiljanic in the paragraph right above yours talks about at line 3 some experience by the staff war exercises of 1994, and he also makes a reference to staff war exercises in the last two years. There were staff war exercises between 1987 and 1998, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994, 5, 6 I was not at the General Staff, and even if something like that existed, I really didn't know that. I didn't work in the General Staff at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the last document I want to ask you about, this is P929. This -- the collegium session of the Supreme Command Staff held on 9 April 1999, and you were listed as being one of the attendees. Do you remember this collegium meeting on the 9th of April? There was a directive that was issued as a result of this collegium meeting, yeah?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would like to go to page 38 of the English and it starts at the bottom of page 45 in the B/C/S. I have a hard copy of this as well, General, that may help. And, General, I've highlighted in pink the bottom of the page and the top of the next page the part that I'm going to ask you about. But let me refresh your memory. Earlier in this meeting General Krga and General Kovacevic and others are talking about what's happened in the first 17 days of the NATO air-strikes and about the current situation. And the general assessment I think General Kovacevic says: "We can sustain another seven to ten days ..." This is based on all kinds of logistical situations. And the discussion seems to be centring around coming up with some proposals about what should be done, one of the proposals is trying to go to the political leadership and have them pursue the possibility of reach a negotiated settlement of the conflict. The part I'm talking about General Ojdanic is speaking and he says: "I mentioned that a conclusion should be given which will confirm how that will affect the possibility of continuing the armed struggle, particularly from the perspective of time, to conduct an armed struggle in conditions of the predicted further course of the war. As for me, as early as tomorrow I will ask the Supreme Command to thoroughly acquaint itself," or themselves, "with this material regardless of how extensive it is and I think it will not be very extensive. I will suggest that after that in a group determined by the supreme commander," was how it was translated, "in a previous discussion, the president briefed that group to a lesser extent on the stands, assessments, conclusions, and proposals of the staff of the Supreme Command as regards what should be done at this time." From an earlier answer of yours, I understood you to be saying that the Supreme Command during the time of war in 1999 was the Supreme Command Staff; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What was your understanding about who made up the Supreme Command during the state of war? We're clear that President Milosevic was the supreme commander and we know that General Ojdanic was the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command Staff. But who were the members of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat once again what I've already said. As far as I know the regulations on this issue, what the Supreme Command is did not exist and I added that in my mind, that was my personal feeling, I always saw the Supreme Defence Council as the Supreme Command, but I have no article of any regulation or law to refer you to to corroborate that. That was my personal feeling based on the constitutional provision that based on their decisions the president commands the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And prior to the war, the Supreme Defence Council consisted of President Milosevic, President Milutinovic, and President Djukanovic, correct? Is that your understanding of who the members of the Supreme Defence Council were?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think we were talking over each other and your answer was not interpreted. Could you say it again.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, these two [as interpreted] were in the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why was that question related to prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, because it was called Supreme Defence Council before the war. It's the Prosecution's position that at least by some once the state of war started it was called the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 25, 17 I believe the witness says that I know three of -- that these three were in the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic -- sorry -- Mr. Fila, why --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I first seek your permission before I ask the question definitely, as I did yesterday. My learned colleague raised two issues that did not stem from the examination-in-chief and did not bring the thing to its close. That's why I want to ask the question. If you recall, a name of a high-ranking officer who was here was mentioned in private session and we didn't get to hear what this was all about. That's the first question I wanted to ask because he testified before this court and I wanted to check what was going on. And the second issue is the issue of the documents that appeared before this Court, as Mr. Hannis said, he indicated that they were used by the Defence. There are documents that are used by the Prosecution that are not from here and it seems the Prosecution doesn't mind that. And I simply wanted to note that both parties are exhibiting documents that do not stem from the official cooperation, and I wanted the witness to clarify how that came to happen. These are the two issues that I wanted to clarify, and if we can't do that, I want to apologise for any time that was wasted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I don't have an objection. I'm not sure what the concern is about. It was clear that regarding that unnamed individual the issue was dealing with whether or not a waiver should be issued for that person to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was left hanging in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was conscious of that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any reason why that should have been in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, because there -- part of the answer was a suggestion that the waiver was not being granted because it was their view that that person had revealed state secrets. Now, I don't know whether that exposes that person to some sort of prosecution in the domestic jurisdiction, but that's why I asked for private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall allow you to deal with both matters, Mr. Fila, and we'll go into private session so that you can deal with the first one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Second question, General: As for your commission you heard from the Trial Chamber and from the Prosecutor that some people said that this was a commission that was, therefore, obstructing work and that you were the anti-Hague lobby, and so on. At the Slobodan Milosevic trial the OTP said when Geza Farkas testified that the commission tried to hide the existence of different things like the Joint Command and whatever. And finally the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis, said to you that there were some documents that came up with General Delic and perhaps some others that were given to this Trial Chamber, apart from you. General, I'd like to tell you something, let us just add something else to this story, the OTP showed different documents here without stamps, without signatures, without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This isn't the time for a speech. You must have a specific question. Please, you're going to devalue any answer you get if you give a speech to the witness about all the possible answers he might give you. So let's cut to the chase. Get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, I'm about to wrap-up, Your Honour. That wasn't my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Specific question, what is the difference between the documents that you submit and all those various documents that keep showing up, being submitted by the Defence, by the OTP, by an international organisation, by such and such, whatever?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents that were copies that were sent through the commission to the National Council for Cooperation with the Tribunal were marked on each page which guaranteed their authenticity and reliability that they were faithful to their respective originals. We, too, had information that documents were following other paths, too, and we warned all the Defence teams, those who were in touch with us and kept -- General Gojovic also warned Mr. Nice that should the commission be required to acknowledge a single document that didn't follow this regular route with no prior verification, it would refuse to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it possible, and that is the key issue, that certain documents that simply showed up, let's talk Defence documents, let's not rile the OTP right now. Would it be possible to check their authenticity by forwarding these documents to you now or then, and then you would tell us whether this was a copy of the document in the original was supposed to be stored in the military archives or perhaps still being used?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After General Gojovic's warning to Mr. Nice, we received over a hundred documents with very specific information, state secrets, such and such number, such and such a date, the header being this or that, and then forward this to the OTP. Obviously the inference we drew based on this is that in some way they had already received these documents; how, I have no idea. In what form, I have no idea. Were those complete documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How about trying to answer the you were being asked which is: If there was a way which documents which don't appear to have come from the commission were submitted they could now be verified? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it's always possible to verify this sort of thing, that shouldn't be a problem. There's the archives, there's the documents, and it's always possible to verify, to cross-reference and to contrast two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My last question: The Slobodan Milosevic trial, I think this cropped up in this trial too once or twice or even three times or God knows how many times, various notebooks have been turning up, MUP notebooks but army notebooks, too. Well, now, a notebook, would that be a document that is supposed to be in the archives of the military; for example, a general's notebook?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you abide by the regulations, each war log-book of that nature gets a file number, it's filed away and is submitted into the archives. Unfortunately, this rule was not always observed, at least not fully and not in each case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So were we to show you a notebook, not you personally, show the Yugoslav Army a notebook, would it be possible to ascertain whether the original was still there or not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOJE TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no original or copy of a notebook unless somebody actually makes a copy, there is the only the original as long as no copy is made, and again this should have been filed away; if filed away, copies can be made, if not filed away then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [No interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the comment made by Mr. Fila, after which Mr. Fila says:

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions for this witness. I'm just using this opportunity to make a suggestion to Mr. Hannis. Perhaps he should check in his own documents the suggestions that he mentioned from April 1999. It's a General Staff document, it's in the OTP's possession, and it has been -- it had been for at least a year before General Delic showed up for testifying in the Milosevic case. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour. Have a great day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is Branko Zigic, and if I may just point one thing out to the Chamber. There's a group of witnesses on its way, the next four witnesses, and those will be in relation to the evidence of OTP witness, Lakic Djorovic. We have tried to the extent possible to keep their chiefs down to a bare minimum, and these are all 92 ter witnesses. Their statements have already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, what is the exhibit number for this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D528, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zigic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. You shouldn't need any papers if that's what you're looking for. Just leave it until you're asked to produce anything that's necessary. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you state your name for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Branko Zigic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is your profession at the moment, Mr. Zigic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: I'm a retired military officer. I'm a colonel by rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In 1999 during the war, what was your post and rank?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: I was a colonel and I was chief of security of the Belgrade military district headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zigic, did you speak an Ojdanic Defence team investigator? Did you provide a statement to that person on the 5th of January, 2007, that you signed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what about yesterday evening when you arrived in The Hague, did you go through that statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If you were to testify before the Chamber about these issues, would your evidence be identical to that stated in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, to the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You would provide all the same answers to all the questions that you were asked?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this witness's statement as a 92 ter exhibit, and I have no further questions for the witness, this is 3D528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zigic, we'll -- we will put your statement -- we will put your statement on the screen in front of you, and that's 3D528, and I'd like you to look at paragraph 3. Now, could you read the first sentence of paragraph 3, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I didn't know nor did Djorovic tell me that the VJ General Staff for ethnic Albanian soldiers were being blackmailed who resided in Belgrade and other parts of Serbia so that they would not be assigned to war units. I should mention that as chief of the security service in the military district, I" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's enough. Could you read it again, please, just read it slowly again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I'm not aware, nor did Djorovic inform me, that blackmail had been organized in the VJ General Staff for ethnic Albanian soldiers living in Belgrade and other parts of Serbia, so that they would not be assigned to war units."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Does any Defence counsel have cross? No. Mr. Stamp. You'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you first briefly about the system in place. As chief of the security section for the Belgrade military district, your unit would sometimes get information about alleged criminal conduct by soldiers --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think there is something wrong with the mike. The witness is indicating.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your unit would sometimes receive information about alleged criminal conduct by members of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: What concerned the military district command and the military territorial units, that's what I was in charge of. I used my own operative connections and channels to obtain information as to whether anything was happening within or just outside the military district command. If what Mr. Djorovic claims was really happening, it's possible that I would have obtained information from a higher level, from the security administration of the General Staff of the VJ or from the security organ of the General Staff of the VJ. They would have indicated that there was something going on, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll get to that. We'll get to that. I just wanted to know how the system worked. Now, on the basis of the information you had, you would do a preliminary investigation and on the basis of this investigation you might present a criminal report to the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Perhaps the only thing that I would do is I wouldn't express this as a possibility. The fact is that during the war I filed over 20 criminal complaints and charges for crimes that were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the military prosecutor may apply that formal proceedings be initiated against the alleged perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Yes -- or perhaps additional information is sought if there is something that remains unclear. If --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: -- All the facts have not an ascertained, so as soon as one seeks additional information one comes to me; that's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: A formal investigation is conducted by a Judge?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they asked me to obtain additional information, whatever can be obtained in the field, one of my subordinate security officers or I in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, in the course of the investigation they would of course ask for assistance from members of the security sector. Now, the military prosecutor sometimes could initiate proceedings or request that formal proceedings be initiated on the basis of information that he received from other sources apart from you or yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I see in your statement you say that: "The security service submits information to the prosecutor so that an investigation may be launched. It is illogical that the service would submit information to the prosecutor for initiating proceedings and then request him to halt proceedings." You agree with me on the basis of what you just said that it is possible that the military prosecutor and the prosecutor could have initiated proceedings without the information coming from you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Djorovic mentioned some names. Do you know Colonel Kracun?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: My apologies. Kracun is a civilian. He's no colonel and he wasn't from my unit. He was from the 10th VOG -- KOG from Belgrade. So what Djorovic told you is not accurate [Realtime transcript read in error "is accurate"].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you worked with him, didn't you? There were occasions that you had to work with him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: I knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to work with him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: No, no, there was never any need for me to work with him. He worked for the counter-intelligence group and he had nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 38, line 6, what the witness said is what Djorovic told you is not accurate, and the transcript reflects otherwise. I think that should be corrected. What Djorovic told you is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zigic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, were you quoting from the evidence of Djorovic when you described Kracun as lieutenant-colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, as colonel?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact his statement which is Exhibit 2671.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Major Djakonovic is your colleague or was your colleague at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: My deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the Tijanic case, you say that you received information from Captain Zuzevic and you --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Zujevic, the late Zujevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you gave orders that Tijanic was supposed to be arrested immediately if he was to appear and handed over to the military prosecutor along with a criminal report. Was this order made on the basis of preliminary investigation that you or your sector had conducted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: This order was made on the basis of the fact that I was certain that General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic were not getting supplies for the army in that way. They had their regular supply methods. I knew that this was some sort of a shady deal and that they were ordering supplies for their own personal benefit; and later on Djorovic made the same request. Should I repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, I just want to know -- you conducted investigations into these allegations about Tijanic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: No, there was no need. The war was ongoing, there were war profiteers, and I saw Tijanic as one such and that is why I ordered that, to stop him from going to some other companies or some other units of the VJ getting supplies, obtaining supplies, for himself because the army had its own supplies. There was no need to go about it in this way. The late Zujevic told me that he had both the stamps and the signatures of General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic. I was certain that this was, in fact, the case because I knew that these were honourable people and patriots. I was absolutely positive that they would never have done such a thing and that's why I decided to put a stop to this practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are going way beyond what I asked you. Can I ask you this: Did you take statements?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Sir, there is absolutely no need to take any statement from a security official. A security official can report to me in writing or verbally. There is a report, not a statement; statements are taken when errors are made.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think that we have again error in transcript. Page 39, line 14 and 15, completely different sense. I can clarify or Mr. Visnjic will clarify with additional questions, but I think that witness's answer completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's been clarified in subsequent answers that that remark could not possibly apply to Pavkovic or Lazarevic. So I think we can proceed I think satisfactorily. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you receive the report in respect to Tijanic in writing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: -- The late Zujevic, chief of security, in the Paola [phoen] military recruitment office told me this in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So am I to understand that the captain Zujevic told you something about Tijanic and you ordered him to be arrested if he was seen and a criminal record submitted --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Should he turn up again at any of the military recruitment offices in Belgrade, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell me what it is he was alleged to have done, what did Captain Zujevic tell you that he had done?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: He said that Tijanic had been coming to the Paola military recruitment office to seek assistance for VJ units from the Pristina Corps. Tijanic, he said, apparently was in possession of the stamps of General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic, and that is why my reaction was what it was. I knew that was a forgery and could by no means be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you are saying that you are not aware that Tijanic was ever arrested?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One moment, one moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we're hearing nothing of the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But none of that answer has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question was: You said in your statement that you were not aware that Tijanic had been arrested; is that so?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When persons are arrested on your orders, is there a system in place for that to be reported to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I was not in charge for all of Belgrade, only the recruitment offices, or rather, the military district. As for security organs in Belgrade, there are several security organs and military police, too. It's not that I only had military police. I had military police from the reserve, mobilised military police; I did not have active-duty military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you know if your unit, your sector, submitted any report at all to the military prosecutor's office in respect to Tijanic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, is it possible that they could have submitted a report and you would not know about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would have been possible because I was rather busy concerning Bubanj Potok and the volunteers on the one hand. On the other hand, at that time Colonel Milovanovic from the security department of the 1st Army got killed, so I was organizing his funeral for three days. I was also engaged with regard to other activities. It is possible that my deputy was informed about this and that he did not inform me about that, that he forgot or something, but I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at P2684 -- oh, I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a different topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Slightly different, Your Honour. It would not -- be convenient to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll break at this point. Mr. Zigic, we have to break at this stage for 20 minutes for various reasons. Meanwhile, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. The Exhibit Number is 2864, could we just have a quick look at that. And if we could just look at the last page, that's page 5 in the English version and I think that's page 2 in the B/C/S version -- well, page 1 in the B/C/S version, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This, sir, is a response dated the 21st of March, 2007, to a request for information sent by the Office of the Prosecutor here to the relevant authorities in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is this 2864? Could we go to the last page in the English version, and that corresponds to the first and second page in the B/C/S version. Let's look at the first page in the B/C/S version first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You'll see, sir, that there are authorities of the Republic of Serbia has indicated that from the records existing one Milovan Tijanic was the subject of investigations filed by the military prosecutor -- prosecutor's office on the 25th of April, 1999, for the criminal offence of breach of duty under Article 174, paragraph 3 of the FRY penal code and for forgery. So in respect to this person, did you not know that the military prosecutor had initiated an investigation -- in fact, that Lieutenant-Colonel Lakic Djorovic had initiated an investigation against Tijanic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on to page 2 in the B/C/S and we could remain on the same page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You will see that the case was assigned a new number following the end of hostilities, and ultimately the records of the case were destroyed. What I'd like to ask you about that part is that it refers to a Milovan Tijanic and it says: "From military post 9650 Pristina." Do you know what 9650 means?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You know that in the VJ in Serbia various military posts are given numbers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One other thing, Mr. Zigic, in your statement you said that -- that Djurovic never approached you or requested any information that "I did not give him if it was in the service's interest." What do you mean when you say "in the service's interest"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 6 of your statement, the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 3D528 you need on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please read the last sentence of paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is page 2 in the English copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please read it aloud, the last sentence in paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I claim with full responsibility that Djorovic never addressed me or asked for any information without me having provided to that to him if this was in the interest of the service," that is to say if it was in the interest of preventing crime or proving that some criminal crime had taken place, nothing else, those were the interests of the service. If I may proceed. "Djorovic even had a meeting with my subordinate security organs without me being present there, all of this with a view to speeding up information flows and proving the commission of crimes more quickly because the distribution of mail was impeded because they moved very frequently and it was difficult to reach them by phone. So he could communicate directly with security organs of lower-ranking units so that they could file criminal reports more quickly, all of this with a view to having a faster functioning."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have in this further for this witness. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zigic, two questions, one pertains to part of your statement that was interrupted due to technical problems and this is why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Visnjic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djorovic, one of the questions that the Prosecutor put to you, or rather, Mr. Zigic --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Serious mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the questions that the Prosecutor put to you, and you gave an answer, but please explain this to us in detail. In addition to yourself and your own organs, who could have arrested Mr. Tijanic in accordance with an arrest warrant, that is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: Any member of the security organs or the military police in the territory of Belgrade, and I've already said. I had a police company from the reserve that had been mobilised, and there was the military police from the command of the 1st Army, there was the military police from the corps, there was the military police from the defence command of the city of Belgrade, from the armoured brigade, and so on and so forth, not to go into the entire establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question: As for your duties, did it -- did they include that you should follow all the cases that the Prosecution was dealing with and did you have to know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: No, only those where I filed criminal reports or my subordinate security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Third question: Did you ever in any way threaten Djorovic or ask him to act in certain cases in a way which --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That doesn't arise. We have the statement of Djorovic and his evidence as to what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How does that arise from cross-examination, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in all sincerity, it doesn't, so I will withdraw this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zigic. No further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ZIGIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zigic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. Have a nice day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our next witness is Arsenije Katanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our next witness is Arsenije Katanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's also going to be a 92 ter witness. His statement was admitted into evidence as 3D530, 5-3-0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Katanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
