utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Katanic.

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, can you give us your full name and surname for the record.

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: Arsenije Katanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, can you please tell us what your current occupation is.

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: Today I am a lawyer. I have my own law office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What was your occupation in 1999, during the course of the war with NATO?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: During the bombing I was an investigative judge in the military court attached to the command of the military district in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Katanic, on the 18th of January, 2007, did you give a statement to an investigator of General Ojdanic's Defence team, one that you signed in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I did make a statement on the 18th of January, 2007, and I signed it in my own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when you arrived in The Hague, did you have a look at the statement?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had a look at the statement that I had signed on the 18th of January, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm that if you testify before this Court, if you were to testify before this Court and answer the same questions that were put to you on the 18th of January, 2007, you would have provided the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I would have provided the same answers because basically that exactly corresponds to how I see things and how I remember them in relation to what I stated on the 18th of January and what I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is 3D530.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, in your statement in paragraph 4 you say that no one exercised any influence over you in relation to the case of an individual by the name of Tijanic. I want to ask you something else. Yesterday when we talked, you told me that during the war you had some serious cases that you had to deal with and that nobody exercised any pressure --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it's going too far, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, it is a very leading question. I appreciate why you think exactly the same evidence would be given today, but I think in court it should be given in the context of open questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then since it was a leading question anyway, perhaps I should withdraw it and I should let the Prosecutor put his questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Just before that happens, Mr. Katanic, the reference in paragraph 4 is to General Gojovic; is that right -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is similar, Mr. President, but it is Gojkovic, there is a K in between. It is General Gojkovic. At that time he was president of the supreme military court, not Gojovic. Gojovic was at that time, as far as I can remember, discharging other duties. At any rate, it is not the same person. General Gojkovic at that time was president of the supreme military court. I have the statement right here in front of me and it does say Gojkovic with a K.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You conducted the investigations in relation to the allegations against Mr. Tijanic?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you take statements from witnesses?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: In that case, as far as I can remember, yes, but I cannot remember specifically how many witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you take statements from -- a statement at least from Tijanic?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: From Tijanic, yes, of course -- well, look, Tijanic was brought before me because I was an investigating judge. He was brought in by the military police, and there was a request there by the prosecutor who at the time was Mr. Lakic Djorovic, suggesting that he be remanded in custody. Of course I could not have him detained or take any other measures before I hear him. I conducted this hearing and he was remanded into custody and a decision was made for an investigation to start. I can also say that on the previous day Mr. Djorovic ordered me, he told me, since he was the prosecutor, that it was a rather serious case and that our court attached to the military command, the military court, primarily dealt with Article 214 of the then-criminal code of the SFRY, and that had to do with dodging the draft, military obligations, and this was not directly related to Article 214. Somebody told, or rather, Djorovic said that it was a more important case, a rather important case; however, when the investigation began I saw that it was truly insignificant. It proved to be a truly insignificant case. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: -- That is as much as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And much is in your statement -- much of what you said is in your statement. One of the allegations against him was that he was in possession of documents purporting to have come from the chief -- the command of the 3rd Corps and the command of the Pristina -- the command of the 3rd Army and the command of the Pristina Corps. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: I don't recall precisely. I know that he was suspected of something of that kind and that I as the investigating judge did check that. I sent memos in order to verify whether this was really authentic because Mr. Tijanic looked - how should I put it? - he didn't look as a person who would be able to do anything of any major importance for anyone because he was in his mental and physical abilities not so good and he couldn't do things even for himself, let alone help anyone else, and that was what we were able to ascertain in the investigation. So the allegations that he had some certificates and that he had been authorised by anyone to gather any aid, that was all refuted. That was really very frivolous charge at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm confused at the moment about whether you're saying the charge was a minor charge or the evidence showed that he was innocent. Because we've had evidence from the head of the security of the Belgrade district that this was a very serious charge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at that time when I got the case in my capacity as the investigating judge, I get the case, when I get the request to conduct an investigation from the prosecutor, in this case it was Lakic Djorovic, or when a criminal report comes in from the military police, at that point in that document this was painted as a much more serious offence, a much more substantial thing than it turned out to have been the case. Afterwards, after the investigation was conducted and all the evidence was gathered, it turned out later that there was no great danger to the society involved in that case and there was no evidence that would mean that this person would have to remain in custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was it that you ultimately established he had done that was so minor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the investigation was completed, during the investigation as far as I can remember I questioned a few witnesses and gathered all the necessary documents, and I completed the investigation, submitting the file to the competent Prosecutor. After a while, the Prosecutor decided not to prosecute and I was bound by the law to put a stop to the criminal proceedings and to the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you not answer my question? What was it that you ultimately established he had done that was so minor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, during the investigation I cannot draw any conclusions -- I don't know how your function -- your system functions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you can't answer the question, just say so; but if you can help us by telling us what this very minor offence was, it would be of great assistance in assessing the various versions that are being presented to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, given that the investigation was stopped and given that the prosecutor decided not to prosecute, the evidence was so insignificant, it was impossible to use it to prove the criminal offence. I can't remember what the criminal offence was, but the evidence was so insignificant that the investigation had to be stopped. The evidence and the entire case, everything that was said, everything that was found and determined in that -- in the proceedings resulted in this conclusion that I made that this was an insignificant case. And after the completion of the investigation, the prosecutor formulated this by saying that there was no need for any further investigation, and he decided not to prosecute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I would also interrupt here to ask you a question, sir. Now, you remember quite details of the file, but you do not remember the facts as to what were the allegations so that you came to the conclusion on the basis of the record that the -- these were very insignificant. I mean, it's -- you ought to know what were -- what was alleged against him, what were the accusations, if you know everything else on the file.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps it is my fault because of the way in which I tried to explain this to you. This man Tijanic stuck in my mind as an individual -- as a man of few abilities, of little power, and this is why I remember him in that way, because the prosecutor painted him in quite opposite colours, saying this is crime, abuse of this nature or that, and that is why -- that's why I remember it because there was this terrible picture, and once we got into the case it turned out that there was nothing. That is why I remember the case. Now, if you want to ask me what he was charged with, I don't know the details, but I know that these were insignificant things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You don't know what was against him? I mean, it's only then that we can find out if it was serious or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the person you say who decided to withdraw the charges was the acting deputy military prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. The procedure is as follows. The prosecutor puts in a request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, I don't need any more information than simply an answer to the question that I'm asking you. Can you help on the date that that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I forgot. A lot of time has passed. I know that the state of war was ended and I know that this case was then put before a military court. It was no longer the wartime court at the district command but it was then transferred to the military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have all that in your statement. If you can just confine yourself, please, to answering the specific questions we're asking you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long did he remain in custody or in detention?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: I can't recall that. I really can't recall that, but I don't think it was a long time but I really can't remember. I know for sure that he was in detention for a while and that he -- that a defence counsel was appointed to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we quickly have a look at -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give us a moment, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P2936.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while this is being brought up can I ask you about how long would files in a case of this nature be kept in the archives before they are destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: Well, I really can't tell you. I am not the archive keeper. I used to be a judge and now I'm a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I could just tell you that document is a response from the authorities of the Republic of Serbia in respect to a request that the Office of the Prosecutor here made and it is dated the 17th of July, 2007, and it indicates --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The English -- and I'm referring now to page 2 of the English copy which corresponds to page 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That indicates that the court files were destroyed in 2003, the files in respect to the case against Tijanic. When did you leave the military service?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: I left the military service in the year 2000, in September, about a year after the air-strikes against my country ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know the circumstances under which these records, the records of your investigation, were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: Of course not because, as I said, at that time I already had my own law office. If I may, I can answer based on my recollection. I think that this case was discontinued in 1999 already, I think by the end of 1999 that case was already discontinued. The decision on the discontinuation became final, which means that in accordance with the practice in the courts it was archived. I don't know what happened with that case afterwards because this is outside of my purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at the last page of the document in the English version, and I think that's the last two pages of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With the help of the usher could I hand you a copy. These are the records from a log-book if you look at the last two pages. What you have there is a log-book referring to the case file and the destruction of the file that was submitted to us by the authorities of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see here 1999, I think it says the 1st of June, -- I can't really read whether it's 2002 or 2003, and the destruction is in 2003. Yes, yes. So it was discontinued sometime in 1999 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: What page? I don't know what page you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: First page of the log-book you have there, the log-book is in handwriting, it indicates that the charges dismissed in May 2000.

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately. I said by the end of 1999. It's possible that it may have been in May 2000. I know that I was still at the court. That case remained my case right from the beginning. I was the first person, the first judge, to see Tijanic and I put a stop to the proceedings. From the beginning to the end. I remember that the case was discontinued. I remember that Mr. Djorovic was the prosecutor. I don't know who the deputy was, but the prosecutor right at the beginning was Djorovic and that was the case throughout the time when I was in the war court, or rather, until he was transferred to the other post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. You have given me much more than an answer to what I was asking. Now, if you look at item 5, items 4 and 5, you will see that it's related to Milovan Tijanic, a sergeant first class. Is the sergeant first class in the VJ, the person you described as being of limited physical and mental abilities who couldn't do anything for himself?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was possible because he was in the reserve force. The reserve force included so many different people that I as a judge saw all kinds of people, from intellectuals to people of meager physical and mental abilities such as Mr. Tijanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But do you remember -- do you recall that he was a sergeant first class? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: -- He looked like an ordinary reserve soldier. That was the impression that I had. I don't recall any rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It also says that he was from military post 9650 Pristina. Can you tell us what the 9650 designates?

utterances.speaker: ARSENIJE KATANIC
utterances.text: I can't recall that, but I assume that it was in the Pristina jurisdiction. I was in Belgrade. I was a judge in Belgrade at the military district command, and that was not the military post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further for the witness. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Katanic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our next witness is Djordje Strunjas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the statement number in this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Strunjas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined been behalf of Mr. Ojdanic by Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Strunjas. Could you please -- actually, I can see that in your statement you retired in 2004 with a rank of a colonel?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What were your duties in 1999 during the state of war?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: In 1998 I was the deputy chief of the administration for international arms control.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: When the combat operations started at the beginning of the aggression, I was transferred to Kumbor to the navy command where I worked as a staff officer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to move closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Visnjic. Could you move closer to the microphone, Mr. Strunjas, it will help the interpreters greatly. Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your last name, Strunjas, it's relatively rare; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether in 1999 there were any other persons with the same surname, Strunjas, working in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 11th of January, 2007, you gave a statement to an investigator of General Ojdanic's Defence and you signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: After your arrival in The Hague were you able to inspect that statement?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If you were to testify before the Court, would you have answered the questions asked of you in the same manner, in the way that you did in the statement?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to tender 3D529, that is the statement made by this witness on the 11th of January, 2007, and I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Strunjas, you'll now be cross-examined on behalf of the Prosecution by Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I decided to just stay here and ask my questions from this location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you just said that you would answer questions today the same as what you said in your statement from January 2007, and I note that in your statement of January 2007 you said that you went to Kumbor on 6 May 1999. Is that when you first went to the navy, in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Well, that's what I just confirmed a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the question was: "And in 1999 you said when the combat operations started at the beginning of the aggression I was transferred to Kumbor to the navy command where I worked as a staff officer." You do know that the aggression started on the 24th of March, 1999, correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So where were you between the 24th of March and the 6th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: I was in Belgrade. I was in Belgrade at the General Staff, but I did not have any duties because the institution where I worked did not have its wartime formation, wartime establishment, rather, we only had the peacetime establishment. And until my wartime assignment was determined, I was in Belgrade. This was a month, a bit longer than a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Even though the war had started, you were sitting there for several weeks before you got the a wartime assignment?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to fill in some gaps in your background from your statement. It says that you were in Pec between 1986 and 1989. Can you tell us what your rank was and what your job was during that time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: I was a major. I was the commander of a motorised battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which one, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: That was the 2nd Battalion of the 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was your immediate superior at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: My immediate superior is the late-Colonel Slavisoje Kosti [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from 1988 to 1994 your statement says you were in Pristina. Can you tell us what your rank was and what your job was during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Yes. I was lieutenant-colonel, and I worked at the corps command as the chief of the operations centre, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was the head of the Pristina Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: The corps commander, unfortunately also no longer alive, his name is Veso Srdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you tell us from 1994 to 1999 you were with the General Staff of the VJ, correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I served in the operations administration of the General Staff, and I held the rank of a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you held that job from 1996 until sometime in 1999 when you went to work for the arms control administration?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: I think there is a misunderstanding there, it was before 1994 and 1996 that I was with the operations administration, and from 1996 on I was with the international arms control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You're right, I misread that. Who were -- who were your superiors -- who was your superior officer when you were in the operations administration until 1996?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Yes, General Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Miodrag Simic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from 1996 until 1999 when you went to the naval posting in the arms control administration who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Colonel Cedomir Gnjilanovic unfortunately, also, no longer among us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were your duties in the arms control administration?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: At the time the arms control administration was in charge of the implementation of state and military commitments based on the Dayton Peace Accords, paragraph 4 of the accords, more specifically, which envisaged certain military restrictions to be imposed on the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And between January -- let's say between the 1st of January, 1999, and the 5th of May, 1999, before you went off to Kumbor, what -- can you describe briefly for us what you did in your job on a day-to-day basis?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: If that's relevant for these proceedings, I can explain that, sir, briefly. First of all, I was not involved in any peacetime assignments performed by my administration, but this was a wartime assignment and all our commitments that stemmed from the Dayton Accords were frozen until such time as combat operations had drawn to a close. I regularly reported to work every morning. We worked in several different military facilities and buildings, but I did not have any special assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I'm still a little bit at a loss. Let's say between January 1st and the 24th of March, when the aggression started, what did you do? You came in to work, but what was your work?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Well, we had our own internal plans, based on which we did some work here and there. For example, educational assignments, we studied certain things, we drew up certain things, but this would normally take no more than several hours a day. I did not have any special assignment, but I see that you're pressing me. Believe me, I would tell you if there was something worth reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And between the 24th of March, when the aggression started, and the first week in May, when you went to Kumbor, what did you do during that time, the same?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: The same thing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: There were many officers attached to these military institutions that simply had no war establishment. We were awaiting our assignments, and as you suggest, I was simply off duty for several weeks where I had nothing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell me where geographically are the military sectors of Zemun - I'm sorry, my pronunciation is not very good - Zemun?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Palilula?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Novi Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: I know Novi Belgrade as a city, but not the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about a military sector? I understand there's a difference between a military district and a military sector; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand that. Military district is higher up than the military sector. Where was the command of the Belgrade military sector, I don't know. I suppose it was at Nemanjina Street number 9, but I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And aren't these three sectors, Zemun, Palilula, and Novi Belgrade all within the greater military district of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have -- in your position, did you have any contacts or dealings with VJ security officers or personnel -- including colleagues and former academy classmates, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us that you're the only person named Strunjas on the General Staff, correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know, sir, is it -- is it a rare name or a common name? Are there other people with your family name in the VJ at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Well, I think there was another one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know what rank he held and where he worked?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: No, not really. We're not related. I don't know. I wasn't in touch with that person. We didn't know each other, but I heard of someone by that name, Strunjas, who I think was working somewhere around Uzice in a place called Kremna. I think that's where he worked, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what rank he held?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: I assume he was my junior, bailiff lieutenant, a captain maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, do you know what VJ body or what administration in the VJ would have information about Albanian soldiers in the VJ or in the VJ reserve. Who was responsible for that? Who kept those kind of records?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Well, the question is not very specific; nevertheless, I believe I know what you're trying to ask me, and I hereby inform you that any information on military conscripts, any military conscripts not just ethnic Albanians, is something that is normally in the possession of military sectors. They have all the relevant documents, files, personal files, records in relation to all military conscripts, not just ethnic Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Is that information that is accessible by members of the General Staff of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Accessible to some, I suppose. There are sectors within the General Staff that in functional terms deal with mobilisation, organizing the army, and they probably have access to that, but in my career and in the posts that I held, I never had anything to do with that type of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You first heard about the allegations of Colonel Djorovic about you allegedly being involved in some sort of ring extorting or blackmailing Albanian members of the VJ or conscripts? You first found out about that, when, in January of this year?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Yes, and I was surprised and embittered. I felt that way for a while. This really affected me. I would never have done anything like that nor did I, indeed, do anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't know Colonel Djorovic at all, do you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You -- so you -- since you don't know him, I assume that you know of no prior grudge or bad dealings that would be a motive for him to accuse you of something you didn't do?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: It might be, but I never worked with him, never met him formally or informally, and I can't quite understand why my name was dropped in that particular context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's why I asked the question, sir. I can't quite understand why if you didn't know him and there was no prior grudge, why would Colonel Djorovic come here under oath and say he had information about you being involved in such a thing and how would he pick your name out of all the possible names in the world? Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: I don't understand. As a witness, I can only tell the truth, I can only tell you about facts, and I cannot base my evidence on speculation or assessments as to why someone might do this or might not do that. It is under oath that I'm telling you this. I was never involved in anything like that nor could I possibly have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I understand your answer to be that you were not, but you say you could not possibly have been. I suggest to you, sir, that you could have been because you didn't have all that much work to do during that time-period, based on your description of your job. You were in Belgrade, you were part of the General Staff which you told me was a body where there were people who might have access to that kind of information. So in terms of opportunity to commit the alleged crime, you did have the opportunity, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: Well, in addition to the fact that there is the time-frame, a time-line for this, that is true. The only coincidence is the time-frame, but everything else you're saying is untenable. None of the other conditions had been met and these allegations are anything but true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned the time-frame, that's the other thing that strikes me as interesting, sir, is that in Colonel Djorovic's statement he indicated this information came to him in April or May. And in your statement you were -- perhaps you just simply weren't asked, but you didn't mention where you were between January of 1999 and May the 6th of 1999 and you didn't mention it when Mr. Visnjic first asked you a question. So are you trying to hide what you were doing between January and May of 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: No, quite the contrary. I'm being entirely sincere and I didn't have an establishment function at the time, but I did report to work every morning. I spent all this time with the people I normally worked with, and I was always there. I could have been checked upon by my superiors by whichever units were in charge of preventing crimes such as the one that is being insinuated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just one final question then. Can you give us the names of the people that you dealt with on a daily basis during that time-period? Just give us the names of three or four people that you were working with every day between January and May of 1999.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE STRUNJAS
utterances.text: I can name a number of people, those were people from my administration, and I will give you a couple of names. For example, my colleagues Colonel Radomir Vujkovic, Colonel Milun Ljubicic, Dragan Todorovic, Captain Dejan Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Strunjas, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Our next witness is Milos Spasojevic. His statement is 3D532.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I read this? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you state your name for the record, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Milos Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasojevic, on the 9th of January, 2007, did you speak to an Ojdanic Defence team investigator, following which a statement was drawn up that you signed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about yesterday, following your arrival in The Hague, did you go through that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Indeed I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were you to be asked the same questions before the Trial Chamber now, would your answers remain the same as those provided in the statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours this is Defence Exhibit 3D532 and I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Spasojevic, you will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Spasojevic. Your statement says from your graduation from law school from 1984 to 2005 you worked at the supreme military court and the military court in Belgrade. Can you tell us how your time was spent between 1995 and May of 1999 at the supreme military court; what was your work there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor, between 1994, May more specifically, you mentioned 1995, but in actual fact this period started in May 1994 to 1999, I worked with the -- I was a lawyer and I had a law practice in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you not a member of the military? Did you have a private law practice? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I was not a member of the military. I had my own office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And so when your statement says you worked at the supreme military court and the military court in Belgrade, does that mean you appeared before that court representing soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, but my statement you must see it in a different light. As of 1986 and all the way until 1994, May 1994, throughout my time with the military I did work for the supreme military court and the Belgrade military court. I appeared before those courts also after this when I had my own private office. But when I talked about me working for the military -- supreme military court and the Belgrade military court, I meant the period between 1986 and 1994, I was professionally involved with those two institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm confused because your statement says you graduated from the law school in 1984 and then it says from then until 2005 "I worked at the supreme military court and the military court in Belgrade." Now, from 1984 until 1986 what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the period that I spent working with the Skopje military court, it was a "stage." Prior to my assumption of a position within the military judiciary to the military court, this was a "stage" at the Skopje military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You may need to help us out with what this was at the Skopje military court. I hear you saying something that sounds like "stoj" but we're not getting an interpretation and I don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Having obtained my diploma at the faculty of law and having started my work as a lawyer, I was already a professional military person in the infantry. I took my degree at the faculty of law and I asked to be transferred to a legal job. They allowed this, but according to the procedures at the time you had to do an internship, some sort of practical experience, work, before you assumed an appropriate post within the military judiciary, and this is precisely the sort of "stage" or internship that I did in Skopje at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That clears that up. So did you go to law school while you were in the military?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I guess I should have started -- when did you first join the military?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I first joined the military on the 14th of July, 1974, having completed the military school for land forces, ground forces, in Sarajevo, the 1st Garrison where I served was in Bitolje. I'm not sure if you want me to elaborate on that or not, if so, please state so, that's 1984; and I graduated. Is that the period you're looking into, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your answer was translated as you joined the military on the 14th of July, 1974, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after graduation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then you told us I think from May 1994 -- well, up until May 1994 you were in the military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then you had a private law practice until I think May of 1999; is that right? Did you retire from the military in 1994 or go on reserve status or what?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. On the 31st of April, more specifically, or the 1st of May, 1994, which I can't quite remember, but I think it was on the 31st of April, 1994, I filed a request to terminate my professional military service. Obviously I became a reservist from that moment on in theory and I started my own private law practice. On the 24th of March, 1999, when the attack on Serbia and Montenegro began, I volunteered, since at the time I did not have an actual war assignment, I volunteered, as I say, to the military court in Belgrade because I had earlier worked for that court and I now wanted to do something there during the war that I was qualified for. I was told that the court was fully manned at the time under the war establishment and that my involvement was not needed. I then asked to be given another duty that I was qualified for. I am a lawyer, after all, so I went to the legal administration of the defence ministry and I was awarded a position there. If necessary, I can go further into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: What else I did throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have some other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have maybe 20 more minutes. I don't know if you want to break or press on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we should break, Mr. Hannis. What we shall do -- just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Spasojevic, we need to have a break at this stage for half an hour. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and return again -- you'll come back again at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Spasojevic, you say in your statement that you knew Lieutenant-Colonel Djurovic from before. Do you recall when you first met him and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of all the time that's gone by, it would be difficult for you to get an accurate answer from me now to that particular question from me now but I will try to remember as much as I can. It is possible that it was approximately in 1990 or 1991 in this building in Mirijevo 12.58.54 where I live, this is part of a neighbourhood. These are apartments that were provided to the military. His best man lived this, his name was Mirko Kujacic. He was a lawyer, too. He worked at the supreme military court at that time together with me, and on one occasion he introduced me to Lieutenant-Colonel Djurovic. I think that he then worked at the legal administration of the Ministry of Defence, and if I remember correctly it is quite possible that that was our only contact of this nature. During the course of our work we did not have any contact; that is to say that officially we never had any contacts at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. So you never had any difficulties or disagreements or problems with him prior to May of 1999; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were appointed in May 1999 to your position to be the military prosecutor for the Pristina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who picked you for that job?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I can give you a precise answer to that question. This is a question that has to do with personnel, and that is decided upon by organs at the General Staff, those that have to do with the appointment of such personnel in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if that was a new position at the time or were you replacing someone who had previously been doing the job?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: As for this position, or rather, this duty, I replaced the person who discharged that duty before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who that was by name and rank?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Captain Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall right now. Before this particular duty, he worked at the military court in Nis. I did not have personal contact with him, so I cannot recall his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why he was leaving that position, was he being kicked out or was he being promoted or did he -- did his term run out? Do you know why there was a need for him to be replaced?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can just assume what the reason might have been why he was replaced from that particular post. Since this replacement took place immediately after the control that was carried out by the chief of the legal administration of the General Staff of the Army of Serbia and Montenegro, so I assume that perhaps they were not fully satisfied with his work. I would like to note that this is just an assumption on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was the chief of the legal administration at that time when the control was carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel-General Radomir Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you ever see a written report of that control that was done prior to Captain Djorovic leaving the position?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Captain Djordjevic [as interpreted] was duty-bound in relation to this control to compile an official report about the work of the prosecutor. If you are referring to that document, I haven't seen that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was actually --

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, the control had to do with the regular control under such circumstances. In addition to that prosecutor's office, at the same time control was carried out of the prosecutor's office in the military district in Pristina and both courts that functioned in Pristina at the time; that is to say the military court attached to the corps command and the one attached to the other command. So it wasn't a targeted control; it was carried out at all the others that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'm assuming, perhaps incorrectly, that there was some sort of report written about that control about all of those courts; and if there was, that's the document I'm asking if you ever saw?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen such a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I assume -- well, I assume that this kind of report was compiled by the organs who had carried out the control, but this report was not accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's good enough. You've answered the question. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you'll try and give me short answers, I'll try and speed this up and get to it shortly. You mentioned in paragraph 3 of your statement, you say when you arrived in Pristina that you - and I think you mean you and Colonel Djorovic - were not called by the state security organs as Djorovic says in item -- paragraph 32 of his statement. Are you saying that you were never called by state security organs after your arrival?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: It is quite certain -- well, I mean as far as this statement is concerned, Mr. Djorovic's statement, it is quite inaccurate. It absolutely does not correspond to the truth. I stand by the statement that I gave in writing. May I just clarify that there is something very illogical in this statement in view of the position of the prosecutor and the position of security organs. According to the Law on Criminal Procedure, or rather, the criminal code of the Republic of Serbia that was in force then, security organs are functionally subordinated to the military prosecutor, and the military prosecutor is the one who engages for the purposes of uncovering crimes and prosecuting crimes he engages organs of the military police inter alia. So it is totally unusual and not customary for security organs to address the military prosecutor and to call him; that can only happen in a private context but not certainly in an official context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So now can we go back to the question that was asked. Were you never after your arrival in Pristina, never ever contacted by state security organs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was contacted not by state security organs but by military security organs; however, only with a view to my service and certain cases where this was necessary, but not in the context referred to by Lieutenant-Colonel Djorovic. The nature of our work, I don't know if you understood the first part of my answer, the nature of the work between the military prosecutor and the security organs is such that by virtue of their work they communicate and there were such contacts every day practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, in paragraph 32 of Colonel Djorovic's statement it doesn't appear to me that he's saying you were contacted in connection with your duties as prosecutors; it just says: "As soon as we were arrived, we were called by state security organs and they were located in an apartment of some expelled Kosovo Albanians." Now, you go on in paragraph 3 to say: "We were not offered any flats that used to belong to Kosovo Albanians that had been expelled." I don't read anything in Colonel Djorovic's statement to be claiming that any such offer was made. I'm curious why you're saying you weren't offering any flattings; Djorovic is not saying that you were. Did you misunderstand that or is there a problem between the translation between the B/C/S and my English version?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: In my response I did not refer to any offer pertaining to apartments. If that was your understanding, then it has to do with inadequate interpretation. Your previous questions did not pertain to apartments or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me hand you the B/C/S version of your statement and ask you to read it, maybe it is a translation problem, it's paragraph 3 and it's the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: May I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to this sentence: "I lived at my deputy's, Dragan Zivica's" -- is that the part you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, it should be the sentence prior to that, if my English is correct.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: "Prior to our arrival in Pristina we were not called by the security organs, the DB organs," is that the part you're referring to. "Upon our arriving we were not called by the security organs" as Lakic Djorovic claims in his statement, in paragraph 32, "we were not offered any flats of expelled Kosovo Albanians." Is that part you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: "I lived at my deputy's Dragan Zivica's and Djorovic was taken by his co-workers" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was translated as saying: "We were not offered any flats that used to belong to Kosovo Albanians ..." My question is: Why did you say that? Djorovic doesn't say in his statement that you were offered flats belonging to expelled Kosovo Albanians; I'm curious why you put that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Probably that is the way the question was presented to me, or rather, that he had stated something like that. I don't know. What I stated is quite certainly correct. During my stay in Pristina, I never lived in a flat of some expelled -- well, first of all, I don't even know who was expelled, let us be clear on that, but I certainly did not live in that kind of apartment. If I stated something like this, I certainly stand by what I said. This is an integral part of my statement and I assume it was written up this way because this kind of question was put to me on the basis of Lieutenant-Colonel Djorovic's statement. He had probably stated something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm telling you, sir, I'm looking at paragraph 32 of his statement and he does not state that. When you were interviewed on the 9th of January, 2007, were you shown Colonel Djorovic's statement and in particular paragraph 32 or was it just described to you by the person who was doing the interview or do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that his entire statement was not shown to me. As far as I can remember now, only parts of his statement were shown to me and then on the basis of that I compiled my own statement. As a matter of fact, I can say that I am sure that his entire statement was not made available to me so I did not write my statement on the basis of his comprehensive statement. It is parts of his statement that were put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one of the parts that was put to you was paragraph 32, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that it would be fair if paragraph 32 of Djorovic's statement were to be shown to the witness in its entirety, because as far as I can see, as this paragraph continues, Djorovic does mention something that has to do with apartments. So perhaps that can be brought into -- P2671.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can deal with that in re-examination, Mr. Visnjic. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 of your statement deals with the issue of a common grave or a mass grave in Orahovac, and you say that you didn't know anything about that and so you couldn't have known anything about a case related to a common grave. Sir, would you allow for the possibility that Colonel Djorovic may have sent a file to you concerning a mass grave in Orahovac, but you either did not receive it or you may have forgotten having seen such a file. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I and Lieutenant-Colonel Djorovic were carrying out duties in two separate prosecutor's offices. He was in the prosecutor's office attached to the military district of Pristina only for a few days, four or five days. I cannot give you the exact timing, but it's not more than four or five days. In view of the nature of the work and the jurisdiction of this prosecutor, or rather, both of these prosecutorial jobs, we could not cooperate because the military district command prosecutor and the prosecutor at the corps command are quite different and they have different powers. I remember that time well, those few days while he was there, I remember that we did not have contacts of this nature; that is to say he never submitted to me any kind of document, or rather, a file.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where were the two of you housed? Were you in the same building or were you in separate buildings? What was that situation?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: We were housed in separate buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How far apart, both in Pristina I take it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Both buildings were in Pristina -- well, say 500 or 600 metres away if I'm able to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor's office of the corps was at the misdemeanours court in Pristina. At one point in time it was opposite the building of the Museum of Kosovo, and the military district prosecutor's office was in a business building, a commercial building, in the centre of Pristina. At that time when Mr. Djorovic was prosecutor, this prosecutor's office where I was a prosecutor and his prosecutor's office, during those three months changed locations in Pristina several times because of the possibility of being bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 further connected to this Orahovac common grave case you mention that Djorovic could not have returned such a file to you and you base that in part because of the case number that he refers to, and you mentioned the case number which had the letters or the initials KV number 106/99. You tell us that the mark KV is a court code for the case and means "in camera." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What would the initials or letters be for a prosecution code case number?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: It would be VTK.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: If it has to do with a known perpetrator; if it's perpetrator unknown then it's KTN. At any rate, KV is a designation for a court file, a court case that is decided upon and that is discussed by a criminal chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I seem to recall having seen the initials KR on some court-related documents; what would that stand for?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: KR is a designation that could be borne by prosecutor's cases and court cases depending on the stage of the proceedings involved. This is before the indictment is issued. At any rate, it has to do with criminal cases. So it is prior to the investigation stage, too, if it came to the court on the basis of a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what would you or personnel in your office have done if you had received delivered to you a file with the letters KV on it, meaning it was an in camera court code case? Would you have kept that file or would you have passed it on to the court as something you shouldn't have?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not say and I don't know why you understood me that way, that this was something I was not supposed to have. The question is a hypothetical one because it does not pertain to a concrete case. How I would act if I got a particular case file depended on the content of that case file itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I ask that question is in your statement at paragraph 5 discussing this court code the English, the last sentence says: "That means that even if there had been such a case, it could not have been with the prosecutor, but with the military court, which Lakic Djorovic, as a lawyer, should know." Now, I understood your last answer to mean just because it has those letters "KV" on it doesn't mean that you couldn't have it for some purposes; am I misunderstanding you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that Lieutenant-Colonel Djorovic said that he submitted a case file with this designation to me, I said in that context what I had said; that is to say that this is a case file that is marked as a court case which does not mean that at some point in time it cannot be in the prosecutor's office. It can certainly be in the prosecutor's office during a certain stage of the proceedings once the criminal chamber passes a decision with regard to a particular case. This decision is most often based on a request submitted by the investigating judge. After such a decision of the criminal chamber, the case is returned to another stage of the proceedings, most often to the investigation stage, because it is the investigating judge that is the one who submits to the chamber the case for it to make an appropriate decision at that stage. I'm saying that it is strange, how come this case would be in the prosecutor's office in view of the stage of the proceedings involved. I did not rule out the possibility that it could not be in the prosecutor's office at any point in time; it can certainly be in the prosecutor's office at a certain stage in the proceedings but not as put by Djorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Two other matters in your statement I want to ask you about. In paragraph 6 you talk about the incident where Colonel Djorovic allegedly beat up his deputy. I just want to confirm that your information about that is second-hand. You weren't present when that event occurred, you didn't see it yourself. All your information is based on what you heard from other people or read somewhere else, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: After this incident, the very next day after the incident --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, do you not understand my question? Can you just say whether that's correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question, but I feel that I need to clarify. The injured party -- well, I was not there at the scene where it happened, I was not present at that incident, but the injured party, the person who was injured by Lieutenant-Colonel Djorovic, who was his deputy at the time, he was the deputy prosecutor at the time, that person, the injured party came to see me in my office the next day after this incident, and he told me himself what had happened in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to paragraph number 7 you say while you were in Kosovo you never drove cars seized from Kosovo Albanians, that you and other organs in the prosecutor's office used vehicles with civilian plates on the roster bearing Yugoslav Army markings, and then there's a question, work papers, and all the necessary documents. Sir, you don't have personal knowledge of where the vehicles you were driving came from prior to your being given control of them, do you? You don't know who might previously have owned the vehicle that you were driving?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: The vehicles that we used, we at the court, came from the sources that I stated here because the data about the vehicles were given to us by the officers from the corps command who were in charge of those affairs. The transport and traffic service officers, they issued appropriate documentation needed for us to use those vehicles during the state of war, so I have first-hand information that those vehicles were -- belonged to known owners. Some of the vehicles, this is not something that I spoke of in my statement, some of the vehicles came from the fleet of the Pristina municipal court, those vehicles had been seized in the course of criminal proceedings against persons who committed certain crimes, and then in accordance with the law the court seized those vehicles because those vehicles had been used in the commission of some crimes. But if you will allow me, I think that it was just one vehicle and it was a Mercedes that had been placed at the disposal by Mrs. Nada Tokovic, who was the president of the Pristina municipal court, so she placed that vehicle at our disposal for our use. I can't recall which one of the judges, but it was just one vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Exhibit 2671, page 9 in B/C/S, could we just clarify one thing relating to a series of questions asked by Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Spasojevic, while we're waiting for this document to come up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it 2671?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. Page 9 in English, that's paragraph 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis asked you about the portion of your statement where you say that allegedly, or rather, I'm trying to find it here, that the state security organs did not call you and that you were not offered any flats that offered to Kosovo Albanians who had been expelled. Now I want to ask you, I don't know if you can see in front of you paragraph 32. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Would you kindly start reading from the second sentence, starting with: "As soon as we arrived ..."

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please read it for the record. We need the exact wording.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: "We were called by the state security organs and they were located in an" --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you just read a bit more slowly starting with "as soon as we arrived ..." And then until the end of this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: "We were called by the state security organs and they were located it an apartment of some expelled Kosovo Albanians."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we then move to page 10, that's the next page in B/C/S, and could we scroll up a little bit. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the first sentence there.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: "I saw with my own eyes the apartment which was taken over by them from expelled Kosovo Albanians."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now could you read the sentence starting with "I didn't want ..."

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: "I did not want to stay in these apartments and Spasojevic took me to a house which was said to be a Serb house."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement in paragraph 3 you said: "We were not offered any flats that used to belong to Kosovo Albanians who had been expelled." What you just read, does that correspond with some interpretation that might present at the first time -- at the same time the question that you provided an answer to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SPASOJEVIC
utterances.text: What I've just read is Mr. Djorovic's statement, and I've already said that it is entirely incorrect. We were never called by any state security organs and we were never offered any accommodation in private homes, and I never offered him the kind of accommodation that he's talking about. So this is completely incorrect. This is just an insinuation, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Spasojevic, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we broke the record and I don't want to push the envelope any further and to set new standards in this institution, but my colleague, Mr. Sepenuk, would like to raise some issues and our next witness will be ready tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. We have a witness scheduled for this Friday, Radomir Gojovic, and we did not put Mr. Gojovic's name on the witness notification last week, because quite frankly we expected to have him next week, but he has very pressing business all next week in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not a problem for us, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, it's a problem with Mr. Hannis, that's why I'm bringing it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So we put him on for this Friday because he must leave for Belgrade on Saturday. Mr. Hannis objects to this because we did give late notice and there's no question we gave late notice because we didn't expect to have him. I think Mr. Hannis was told informally on Monday, we gave informal notification on Tuesday and we filed our formal notification yesterday, and -- but Mr. Hannis says he's unable to get the necessary work done for the cross-examination. I will say this is a 92 ter witness. We will be introducing the testimony from the Milosevic case and the exhibits introduced in the Milosevic case, and that's a very major portion of the points we're making through Mr. Gojovic. There will be additional material, but it's essentially the Milosevic material with certain other matters stressed. But in any event, I believe Mr. Hannis wants to object to -- I think Mr. Hannis has suggested we do the direct and we save the cross until a future time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When will Gojovic again be available?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: He would be available on the 3rd or 4th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you have no other evidence available on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We do, as a matter of fact, we have one other witness scheduled for Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But not for the full day?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Not for the full day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nothing can be advanced to fill the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Not as I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I did object. We got an e-mail that was sent at 9.45 p.m. on Monday and I didn't see it until Tuesday morning, indicating that they wanted to add Mr. Gojovic as a witness for this week. He is a significant witness, Your Honour, probably the primary issue going to the issue of lack of punishment. He did testify in the Milosevic case. Although I think there are only ten exhibits noted on the notification for him, the -- the materials are substantial. I think his prior testimony is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 300 pages of transcript. The exhibits -- I don't know how many pages there are because when I tried to open that document listing the Slobodan Milosevic exhibits I was unable to open it yesterday. So I'm not sure how many pages that is. In total it's about 600 pages because we've been preparing for about ten other witnesses this week, Your Honour, of whom two we learned yesterday, I guess, are not going to be called at least this week. I find myself in a very difficult position trying to be ready and do a professional job of cross-examination on Friday.
