I know we have two witnesses schedule for tomorrow and then in addition to Mr. Gojovic on Friday we do have witness Pantelic scheduled. So it may not even get to be that problem, but I did want to alert Your Honours if we did and if you expect me to complete and conducted my cross-examination on Friday I found that I should alert you that I would be asking for some leave in that regard because of the late notification and the amount of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problems confined to cross-examination so it can be dealt with if and when it arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Indeed and I wanted to give you a heads up on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it may be that its only part of the cross-examination that's affected by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: However, this does give us an opportunity to look at the more general question of time. We know, I think, enough about how things are going now to review the situation, and I would welcome some guidance from counsel about this. We had assumed that there would be ongoing discussions among Defence counsel about the allocation of time, indeed we've said that that should happen. Now, Mr. Visnjic or Mr. Sepenuk, I don't know who's principally dealing with this, has there been discussion in which you have broad parameters agreed about the use of the hours that are available for the presentation of the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no, but we knew that the first two Defences would take up less time than planned, but we didn't have any further consultations than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a real problem because we've obviously proceeded under a misapprehension. Of the 500-and-odd hours estimated by the Defence, we allocated 240, and that means that somewhere between 40 and 50 per cent of what was anticipated was allocated -- in fact, it's little more than 40 per cent. And had we been applying -- or were we to apply that to the original estimate of your case, you could find that next week might be your last week, subject of course to Mr. Ojdanic giving evidence and you've got him scheduled for a week. Now, we have to be conscious of the interests of the later accused as well as the interests of your client, and as far as I can see you're about, apart from the evidence of your own client and the expert listed, you're only about a third, not quite a half way through the witnesses. Now, we appreciate your demonstrating serious efforts to cut down the time in court and to present the evidence in writing, but it may be coming a bit late in the day in your case and that's why it has to be addressed now. If parties are not able to reach broad agreement on the division of time, then we will have to do it for you; and you'll appreciate our reluctance to do that unless it's absolutely necessary. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- it may be less of a problem than you think. The Pavkovic Defence presentation will take significantly less time than the Ojdanic presentation, mostly because we would have had to call some of these witnesses if he hadn't done so, and by the same token we're putting on some witnesses that the Lazarevic Defence would have had to call had we not done so. So all those things are working in your favour, Your Honour. Let me finish -- go ahead, you always get to interrupt. You're the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, please go ahead. I'm happy to listen to anything you think needs to be said first of all and then I'll come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then the other thing our -- the bar table motions that we're all trying to get dealt with, because that would keep us from having to show a bunch of documents to witnesses and I can move through my witnesses really rapidly if I don't have to introduce documents through them and can get them admitted through the bar table. So we're all trying I think really hard to move us into that 240 hour time-period that you have set out. And I don't see a major problem developing, although the Lazarevic and Lukic Defences may disagree with me. But I would hope that that is not such a rigid time-period that the interests of justice are overcome by rigidity and timing that that would keep justice from being done in this case and I don't think that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there are three things to be said there. And one is that it's a generous allocation bearing in mind what happened in the Prosecution case and was designed -- or was based on the anticipation that there would be great deal of coordination, discussion of the time involved among the various parties, and the use of writing to -- in all the areas where that's appropriate. And it's clear -- this is simply a basic statement. It's clear -- it was clear in the Prosecution case, it's clear in Mr. Visnjic's case that there are things which could have been done in writing which haven't been done and they wouldn't have caused any prejudice. So that's number one about the length of time. Number two is that your first point about the witnesses being apparently reduced because of the way in which the case is being presented doesn't really fit the picture I have because there are virtually no witnesses in common -- in fact, if there were a couple at the beginning then that was resolved. So your witnesses, although they may be giving evidence that's helpful to other members of the military, are your witnesses. They do not arise in common with the others. Your third -- the third point that needs to be made is to say that we welcome greatly the efforts to have the documents presented at the bar table and we are giving currently active consideration to that. So I don't think what you've said reassures me entirely about the division of time. Mr. Visnjic's original estimate is a bit longer than yours, and if you were saying to me you're going to be a lot shorter than your estimate, that's fine, but we initially expected you to be at least 50 per cent shorter than your estimate before this exercise started. You can see that if you just look at the basic figures. So you can see it seems to me there's been a bit of burying heads in the sand on this one and we can't allow it to continue. We have to address it in fairness to everyone. Just looking broadly, this is off the top of my head as a broad indication of the sort of thing that we anticipated might happen, the Lukic team have estimated something that would take six months. They've always said to us they thought their case would take three months. So they're probably -- if they can do it in three months, they'll fit in probably just under half of the number of hours that they've actually estimated, that's a very broad brush. There are three military people here, there must be a great deal in common, and therefore we anticipate that their case can be looked at to some extent as an entity, and you've just confirmed that, but by no means an entire entity, each one has its own interest. So we don't expect the whole military case to be the same as the Lukic case but we don't expect it to be three times the Lukic case. You can see the broad indication. Now, if we could be assured that by the end of this year we will be close to finishing the military case, fine, but that's not the picture that's building up just at this minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I neglected to give you an estimate. It would surprise me a great deal if the Pavkovic takes -- case takes two weeks, and I think that would certainly put you in a position where the military case would be finished by the end of the year, should, but our case is not going to be very long, provided we can get the bar table documents taken care of the way we want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a very useful exercise. Now, Mr. Visnjic, I know that you've been looking for information about figures that hasn't been given to you as yet, but taking into account even today's time which in your case is no more than half an hour I imagine, you've done about -- just over 19 hours of examination, if that helps you, but the hours you've allocated to the witnesses yet to be heard in your case, apart from your client and the expert, is 37 hours, twice as much as you've already used. And you've used two and a half weeks. So you have another five weeks plus your client and then there's the expert evidence later. Now, that doesn't fit in even with Mr. Ackerman's schedule. He's, clearly, doing as the first two accused did and focusing on things that are crucial. But you have a different approach as far as we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can give you an estimate, some kind of an estimate now as to when our case would end if that means anything to you. I assume that we will call all the evidence, apart from General Ojdanic's testimony, before the break that is anticipated for the 8th, by that I mean all the witnesses including possibly the expert. Now, of course that would depend on the length of the cross-examination, but I believe that we should be able to do all that before the break starting on the 8th. I don't know how many hours that would take, but if we're talking about 19 to 37 hours, I think we will have a -- we will be able to do a lot of progress. The only reason why I need a break, and that's why I would like to ask you for two, three days before General Ojdanic's evidence, lies in the fact that we practically were unable to consult before the beginning of our Defence case, and that's why I would like to ask for an adjournment of a couple of days to be able to consult with him about his evidence. But his evidence will take substantially less time than indicated in our initial assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You -- I can't let that last remark pass. You had a great deal of time to consult. That was part of the approach that this Chamber has taken to the preparation for and presentation of the case. Were you going to say something, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just to advise Your Honour that we have a difficulty with the Defence military expert because we don't have the English translation of his report yet, and frankly it would be nice to have that in hand before General Ojdanic testifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. One of the -- let's be sure we're on the same wavelength here, Mr. Visnjic. You have two and a half weeks -- less, you have two weeks and two days to the break, one of them is not a complete week. Now, you can only -- your examination-in-chief is going to be no more than eight or nine hours in each of these weeks. So you're -- with the best will in the world continuing the way you're continuing, you'll do another period slightly less than you've done so far in your case. Now, are you saying you will complete the other witnesses other than the expert and Mr. Ojdanic by then?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We may then have to consider his position and --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Including the expert, I meant including the expert -- [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a problem if the translation's not available and you're saying you'll do it even with the expert which is better. We would regard the break as your obvious time to ensure that you've done -- had adequate consultation with Mr. Ojdanic. We would not be contemplating any additional time off than that, and we would also hope -- you've estimated eight hours in his case and I think you should be trying to adhere to no more than that. The one person, above all, we are extremely anxious not to restrict in giving evidence is an accused who chooses to do so. I think we see that as a different position from other evidence; on the other hand, one has to be realistic about it and there is a limit to how many things any accused person can deal with specifically in any detail in a case like this. So we hope you'll bear that in mind in deciding how to present his evidence, but we are conscious of that as a difficulty. Now, if anyone else has anything to say, please say it now, because we will have to reflect on this. This has been very useful and very encouraging - I speak for myself in saying it - it sounds encouraging because it sounds rather different from what I had anticipated before asking. Very well. We shall adjourn now and resume at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of September, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.54 p.m.,
